newsitem.title: CHINA: China firm vows to regain space market confidence.
newsitem.headline: China firm vows to regain space market confidence.

text.p: A top Chinese aerospace company vowed on Thursday to win back the confidence of the world satellite market after several launch failures.
"We have found the reasons for the past failures and we have addressed the problems," said Yu Xianrong, general manager of the space department of China Great Wall Industry Corp.
Yu told Reuters it was too soon to assess what impact China's string of launch failures would have on insurance costs but he believed future successes would help to bring rates down quickly.
China once had a reputation for cheap and reliable commercial space launches but a series of failures, some of them spectacular, have badly tarnished its reputation.
In August, a domestic communications satellite launched aboard a Long March 3 rocket failed to reach proper orbit.
That followed the explosion in February of a Long March 3B rocket carrying an Intel satellite. At least six people were killed and 57 injured while 80 homes were destroyed.
In January 1995 a Long March 2E rocket blew up, destroying the Apstar 2 satellite it was carrying and killing a family of six on the ground.
"We realise that we must raise the reliability of our launch services," said Yu.
"We have spent a lot of time analysing and correcting the problems."
Even without the recent failures, China faced growing competition from Russia and Ukraine, which have made strides in selling their space technology to the commercial sector.
China Great Wall, a trading and manufacturing arm of the state-run China Aerospace Corp, is in charge of satellite launches for foreign customers.
Its next chance to prove itself will be in the first half of this year when it launches a telecommunications satellite for the Philippines.
Great Wall is hoping success will dispel any insurance market anxiety.
Insurance industry officials said premiums could top a hefty 20 percent of the insured value, undermining China's substantial cost advantage on its launch fees.
"Rates go up as soon as you have a failure," said Yu.

"We can't say what the future insurance rates will be," he added. "But international insurers are satisfied with our explanations of the problems and we expect they will join (underwriting syndicates) for future launches."
But in a sign there could be lingering problems, Great Wall's customer would be responsble for obtaining insurance coverage for the satellite on the next launch.

China is also pinning its hopes on plans to launch some 22 satellites by 2001 for the IRIDIUM consortium, which will set up a global telecommunications network using 66 low-orbit satellites. Motorola Corp of the United States has 25 percent of the multi-billion dollar project.
This will mean deployment of more than one satellite on a single launch, reducing costs and substantially expanding the nation's launch record.
"We have to be more competitive in future," said Yu. "There is no alternative."
